summary: Mars Pathfinder is a live web tool that plans a Marswalk for the first astronauts on Mars. It layers data from several NASA missions into one 3D view: MOLA/HRSC global elevation with exaggerated relief, HiRISE 1 m terrain at Gale crater, TES dust cover and thermal inertia, THEMIS day and night infrared shown as heat maps, and the USGS geologic map. The astronaut picks sourced Curiosity science stops and a movement profile. The planner never enters ground steeper than the profile's slope limit, compares climbing over a hill with walking around it by walking time, shows the round trip with work time and the remaining time reserve, and explains every route choice. Close to the walker, an image model (SegFormer-B0) trained on AI4Mars and our own hand-labelled Curiosity Hazcam images proposes rocks, stereo depth confirms them, and the route is redrawn between them; we tested this on 142 real Curiosity frames. We call this pairing of a far satellite route and a near camera route Dual Correction. It matters because orbital maps resolve about 200 m, while a 30 cm step can stop a suited walker. Mars Pathfinder is a research prototype, not a certified safety system.
details:
What it does

Mars Pathfinder is a live web application for planning a Marswalk. It brings data from several NASA missions into one 3D map and plans a walking route that a first crew could follow, from the orbital scale down to individual rocks. It has three modes: Explore (a 3D Mars globe with exaggerated relief, 2,055 named places and switchable condition layers), Plan a route (science stops, movement profile, round trip with time reserve) and Live GPS Test (route guidance on real Curiosity camera frames).

How it works: Dual Correction

Far route (satellite): slope and roughness are computed from the MOLA/HRSC global elevation model (about 200 m) and the HiRISE 1 m terrain model at Gale crater. Each movement profile has a hard slope limit (15 degrees for a walking astronaut); the planner never enters steeper ground. When a hill is in the way, three options are compared: the shortest path up the slope, a balanced path and a detour on gentle ground. Each is converted to walking time with Tobler's hiking function and the fastest is chosen, preferring gentler ground when the difference is only seconds. The Decisions tab explains every choice in plain language. Work time at science stops and the walk back to the start are taken from a time budget, and the remaining reserve is shown.

Near route (camera): a SegFormer-B0 segmentation model, trained on AI4Mars labels and our own hand-labelled Curiosity Hazcam images, proposes rocks. Stereo depth from the same camera decides whether a candidate is really a raised obstacle, and the route is redrawn between confirmed rocks. We tested this on 142 real Curiosity Front Hazcam frames from sols 40 to 150, with recorded rover positions from MSL PLACES.

Conditions layers

TES dust cover and thermal inertia, THEMIS day and night infrared shown as heat maps, the USGS geologic map and a data confidence layer can be switched on and off like layers in a globe viewer. Season, daylight, a noon temperature bound and MSL RAD radiation are shown alongside the plan, each labelled as measurement, historical record or model.

Benefits and impact

Orbital maps resolve about 200 m, but a 30 cm step can stop a suited walker. Mars Pathfinder joins both scales in one plan, shows science targets at the positions Curiosity actually visited, and keeps the time needed to get back in view.

Tools

TypeScript, React and CesiumJS in the browser; Python, FastAPI, NumPy and ONNX Runtime on the server; PyTorch for model training; hosted on Render. Source code: https://github.com/Poyraxx/mars-pathfinder-ai

What we considered

Every number is computed when you ask, and every value carries its source. Walking speed and time budget are planning assumptions, fine detail exists only where HiRISE and rover images exist, and this is a research prototype, not a certified safety system.
